Special attention is paid to the development of students' communicative competence, independent learning skills and digital literacy through the application of artificial intelligence tools to language teaching.

Abstract As Artificial Intelligence (AI) becomes “smarter”, it brings forward more fundamental rather than technical problems to solve, entailing legal, ethical or even philosophical questions. In this session, the core issue of AI “alignment” is investigated under the scope of clarifying the boundaries between human and machine responsibilities, especially in the decision-making process within safety-critical applications. The current legislative status is briefly presented, primarily for the EU and USA, regarding “safe” and “trustworthy” AI, while the role of open-source models, platforms and applications is explored as probably the most important aspect. Furthermore, the moral aspects of fully autonomous AI systems are discussed through the classic “trolley problem”, demonstrating the difficulties of even formulating such tasks for designing AI. Finally, ten core principles of “aligned” AI are summarized and a few suggestions are discussed regarding how these principles may be incorporated in practice towards this direction.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The increasing availability of pretrained Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) models has accelerated the operational adoption of deep learning within geographic information systems. However, models developed in one geographic region frequently experience performance degradation when deployed elsewhere because of geographic domain shift. Although transfer learning is widely used to improve cross-regional model performance, it remains unclear whether improved predictive accuracy alone provides sufficient evidence for trustworthy deployment. This study investigates this question using rooftop solar photovoltaic mapping in Brisbane, Australia, as an operational case study. Esri’s pretrained US Solar Panel Detection model was locally calibrated through transfer learning and evaluated using both development and independent local test datasets within Brisbane. Local calibration substantially improved detection performance, increasing recall from 38.5% to 84.1% on the development dataset, with similar improvements observed on the independent 10-grid test dataset, indicating effective local adaptation within the sampled Brisbane environments. However, independent evaluation and qualitative error analysis revealed persistent false positives, missed detections, and geometric segmentation errors, highlighting residual uncertainty and the limitations of model performance within the evaluated geographic context. These findings suggest that transfer learning can substantially improve detection performance and provide useful evidence for assessing operational trustworthiness, although predictive improvements alone are insufficient to establish trustworthy deployment. By integrating complementary evidence relating to robustness, reliability, generalisation, transparency, and residual uncertainty, this study provides an evidence-based operational approach for assessing pretrained GeoAI models and informing responsible deployment decisions in geographically distinct environments.

Purpose Despite the application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in organizational workflows and business processes, many firms have not achieved improvements in innovation capabilities and value creation. This suggests that capability development depends not only on artificial intelligence (AI) but also on the effective orchestration human and artificial knowledge in work routines and business activities. This study explores the mechanisms underlying human–AI knowledge orchestration (KO) and identifies drivers, inhibitors and boundary conditions shaping managers’ participation. Design/methodology/approach Integrating knowledge orchestration theory and social exchange theory, the study conceptualizes knowledge growth, AI self-efficacy (AISE), perceived organizational support as benefits, execution cost (EC) and knowledge power loss as costs and trust in AI as the moderator. The model is tested using structural equation model with data from 341 managers in AI adopting firms. Findings Knowledge growth, AISE and perceived organizational support positively affect human–AI KO, whereas EC and loss of knowledge power (LKP) have negative impact. Trust in AI strengthens the positive effect of knowledge growth and AISE but unexpectedly exacerbates negative impact of EC and LKP. Social implications This study highlights the importance of fostering trust and addressing barriers in human–AI collaboration, offering insights into the responsible adoption of AI in the workplace. The findings may contribute to more inclusive digital transformation and AI-enabled knowledge management practices. Originality/value By conceptualizing human–AI KO as a dynamic knowledge management process embedded in workflows and business processes, this study advances research at the intersection of AI, knowledge management and business process management. It responds to calls to embed knowledge management in work routines and examine individual-level factors in AI-supported business processes. It reveals the benefit–cost trade-off underlying managers’ participation and provides implications for AI-enabled knowledge management, business process improvement and capability development.

This study investigates the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) service on customer engagement in the Indonesian retail industry, with intention as a mediator and trust as a moderator. A quantitative research design was employed using Structural Equation Modelling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS), with data collected from retail customers across Indonesia who had experience using AI-based services such as chatbots, recommendation systems, and virtual assistants. The findings reveal a significant positive impact of AI service on customer engagement (p < 0.001). Furthermore, intention played a significant mediating role between AI service and customer engagement (p < 0.001), supporting the Theory of Planned Behaviour. Contrary to theoretical expectations, trust was not a significant moderator between AI service and intention (p = 0.331), nor between intention and customer engagement (p = 0.337). The proposed model explained 43% of the variance in customer engagement and 49% of the variance in intention, indicating moderate predictive power. The non-significant moderating role of trust suggests that Indonesian consumers may have developed high trust in digital technologies due to the rapid growth of e-commerce and digital financial services, or that the utilitarian nature of AI services reduces the salience of trust as a boundary condition. These findings offer both theoretical and practical implications regarding the implementation of AI service. Theoretically, the study extends the Theory of Planned Behaviour to AI service adoption in emerging economies and questions trust's generalizability as a moderator. Practically, retailers should invest in AI capabilities and foster positive customer intentions.

This article examines how the coexistence of photographic and AI-generated war imagery reconfigures the conditions of media witnessing (Frosh and Pinchevski 2009). Today’s platformed visual culture is characterized not only by an unprecedented abundance of images, but also by the convergence of images produced through fundamentally different operations: whereas traditional photography registers light from scenes before a camera, generative AI models synthesize photographic-looking images through statistical prediction. Thus, photorealism (Hausken 2024) no longer guarantees indexical registrations of the world. Through reception-oriented analysis of Thomas Hirschhorn’s Pixel-Collages (2015–2016) and Ilkin Huseynov’s Looming Dreams (2023), the article traces how this transformation becomes perceptible in contemporary art. Hirschhorn’s collages engage with poor images (Steyerl 2013a): traditionally produced photographs whose evidentiary meanings are destabilized through postproduction, recirculation, and decontextualization. Huseynov’s AI-generated images, by contrast, depict war without detecting particular events, nevertheless retaining a genealogical relation to photography through their training data and the reproduction of the photographic form. Read sequentially, the works demonstrate that epistemic uncertainty (Chouliaraki 2015) spans rather than separates photographic and synthetic imagery: photographic registration cannot guarantee stable meaning-making, while photographic appearance no longer guarantees that registration even occurred. Bringing Wolfgang Welsch’s concept of derealization into dialogue with theories of new media, centrally the concept of digital witnessing Chouliaraki 2015) and secondary witnessing (Varvia 2024), the article develops the concept of unstable witnessing. This describes a mode of reception in which images remain indispensable to sensing and perceiving distant wars, while intensified exposure and heterogeneous modes of image production make their provenance and evidentiary status increasingly difficult to establish. The artworks do not resolve this uncertainty but render its perceptual operations visible, staging contemporary media witnessing as suspended between trust and distrust, testimony and fabrication, and sense-making and its breakdown.

Large Language Model (LLM) interaction records are increasingly being used as digital evidence for forensics and compliance. However, traditional linear tamper-evident logs cannot capture the complex nonlinear conversation evolution, such as prompt-editing, response regeneration, session deletion, multi-device concurrency, and selective sharing. This study proposes the Verifiable Conversation Transcript (VCT), which models these operations as authenticated account-level state transitions across a three-layer cryptographic structure: Q&A pairs form branch hash chains and branch tails aggregate into session-level Merkle roots (MTRcon). These session-level roots are further aggregated into the account-level Merkle root (MTRacc), which is jointly authenticated by both user and server signatures. The VCT also introduces a serialized deletion protocol, a deterministic merge protocol that preserves concurrent non-deletion updates, a gossip-based fork detection mechanism that produces non-repudiable forensic evidence, and a verifiable sharing protocol that constructs an independent dual-signed share hash chain across disclosed nodes. Based on standard cryptographic assumptions, the VCT guarantees integrity, consistency, share verifiability, and non-repudiation of account-level conversation records. A Python prototype achieves sub-millisecond mean latency under minimal state with short synthetic payloads. With 21 KB per-node payloads, the estimated metadata-to-content ratio is approximately 0.9% across the tested account scales. These results support the computational feasibility of the prototype under the tested conditions and provide practical guidance for the engineering design and optimization of verifiable LLM conversation systems.

Abstract The design of Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been shown to be “unfair” to less-spoken languages and to deepen the digital language divide. Critical sociolinguistic work has also argued that these technologies are not only made possible by prior socio-historical processes of linguistic standardisation, often grounded in European nationalist and colonial projects, but also exacerbate epistemologies of language as “monolithic, monolingual, syntactically standardized systems of meaning” (Schneider, 2024, p. 5). In our paper, we draw on earlier work on the intersections of technology and language policy (Kelly-Holmes, 2019) and bring our respective expertise in critical sociolinguistics and computational linguistics to bear on an interrogation of these arguments. We take two different complexes of non-standard linguistic varieties in our respective repertoires – South Tyrolean dialects, widely used in informal communication in the Italian province of South Tyrol, and varieties of Kurdish across different national contexts – as starting points for an interdisciplinary exploration of the intersections between GenAI, linguistic variation, and language standardisation. Through these case studies, we show that linguistic marginalization in AI systems can arise through different mechanisms: from the limited visibility of dialects within computational infrastructures to the interaction of technological underrepresentation with histories of political and institutional exclusion. We discuss the technical barriers preventing LLMs from processing non-standard varieties, examine how evaluation frameworks reproduce standardization biases, and explore policy implications for diverse actors, thereby contributing to ongoing efforts to develop language technologies that account for linguistic variation and the diverse sociopolitical conditions under which languages and varieties become digitally represented.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Official empirical benchmark and research release for Wake-Sleep Null-Space Consolidation (WS-NSC), an algebraic continual learning framework designed for autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Abstract: Sequential adaptation of Transformers without raw data rehearsal induces catastrophic forgetting. While Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) minimizes memory footprints, merging learned low-rank updates directly into base weights corrupts pre-existing representations. We empirically study Wake-Sleep Null-Space Consolidation (WS-NSC), an algebraic consolidation mechanism that projects low-rank updates onto the empirical orthogonal complement of historical activation covariances. Evaluating SmolLM-135M on a sequential stream (GSM8K → IMDb → AG News) anchored by WikiText-2, we demonstrate that WS-NSC eliminates catastrophic forgetting (-0.39% relative drift vs. +5.83% in direct merge) and halts anchor drift. However, this stability incurs an acute plasticity penalty, reducing retained task gains to 37.7% (ρ=0.90) and 24.4% (ρ=0.95). We show that retaining parameter update norm (~74%) does not guarantee functional retention (~38%), formalizing the empirical trade-off of hard null-space projection in nonlinear Transformers. Code & Benchmark Repository: https://github.com/AkshatRaj00/ws-nsc

Between 2024 and 2026, AI literacy moved from a loosely used phrase to a formal object of international policy. UNESCO, the Digital Education Council, the European Commission and OECD, the OECD's PISA pro‐ gramme and the Council of Europe each published a framework or stand‐ ard defining it. In the same period, school systems began acting on the idea at scale: China set national targets for AI education at every stage of schooling, Boston Public Schools launched AI literacy across its high schools, and New York City paused student-facing generative AI for its younger pupils. This article compares five frameworks and three system- level policies, drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders over the same period. It finds strong agreement on four elements: understanding how AI works, critically evaluating its outputs, using it ethically, and keeping human judgement and agency at the centre. It finds five real differences: how much weight goes on the human dimen‐ sion compared with tool use, whether learners should create and shape AI, whether literacy is general or domain-specific, how it develops with age, and whether choosing not to use AI counts as a competence. The policies show that the hardest problems lie outside the definitions, in teacher capacity and in assessment that can tell knowing about verifica‐ tion from actually verifying. We propose a synthesis model and set out implications for curriculum designers, school leaders and assessment bodies.

Imagine if teachers spent less time drowning in administrative tasks and more time inspiring their students. Fewer hours are spent on grading, lesson planning and scheduling, and more time is devoted to mentoring and engaging with students. Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to make this a reality.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: If a student uses artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in their work, does that necessarily make the work less “original”? This chapter focuses on the notion of originality and argues for a critical examination of its meaning in a time when AI grows more integrated into students’ work processes. The chapter begins by tracing the historical roots of originality, unpacking how its embedded value orientations around individualism have shaped—and continue to influence—current assessment standards and policies in higher education. It then discusses how these traditional understandings of original work not only are becoming untenable but may also be inadequate for preparing students for a future where AI will significantly shape their way of learning, working, and living. The chapter concludes with several pathways to reimagine originality in higher education assessment, highlighting the need for a more inclusive environment for students to produce meaningful work.

The challenge of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) provoked a renewed interest in assessment in higher education and how it might need to change. The problems of assessment and the need for repair existed well before AI appeared on the scene, but they are more pressing now. This chapter focuses on the necessary requirements of assessment regardless of the conditions in which it occurs: assessment for assurance; assessment to guide learning; and assessment to build students’ capacity to make evaluative judgements. It examines these purposes and discusses the implications of the rise of GenAI for each. It considers both policies and practices and concludes that, whatever else needs to be done, a priority is to strengthen students’ capacities to make effective evaluative judgements both about their substantive work and about the use of any AI applications that may aid them.

“Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The recent introduction of automated complimentary upgrades reflects the emerging role of artificial intelligence (AI) in making symbolically meaningful decisions in tourism. We explore consumers’ responses using a thematic analysis of online comments and open-ended survey responses, followed by a quantitative survey to validate findings. Paradoxically, the qualitative analysis reveals that both unbiased decisions and personalization are valued. The quantitative study further shows that lay beliefs about AI are associated with preferences, through procedural and interactional fairness. Only procedural fairness fully mediates the lay beliefs’ association with intention to negotiate out of dissatisfying upgrade decisions. Moreover, desire to be treated as a unique customer weakens the lay beliefs’ association with interactional fairness and the indirect association with preferences. We contribute by revealing how consumers respond when automated agents make symbolically meaningful decisions in the automated preferential treatment context. Firms should prioritize the procedural legitimacy and symbolic framing of automated decisions.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Systems such as Sakana AI's Fugu place one coordinating model in front of several other AI models. The coordinator chooses which model works on each step, asks another model to check the work, and merges the results into one answer. This concept note reads the published papers behind such systems (Trinity and the Conductor) and points to seven places where a chain of this kind can slip: the stop decision that rests on one model's judgment, a very delicate reading signal, a coordinator that can call itself, fixed limits that do not show drift, one worker's slip passed to the next step, a pool of models that changes, and a merged answer that carries no sign of how firm it is. The note then suggests a simple, training-free addition: a warning number that measures how slowly the small everyday wobbles of a few signals settle back, read over a series of runs. It is inversely proportional to the size of the leading eigenvalue, so a rising number shows the chain approaching a tipping point. Three calm states follow: Steady, Watch and Look closer. A computer-decided shunting action then acts without waiting for a person. It moves the doubtful runs to a simpler path or an extra check, while all other runs carry on and nothing is stopped. The note describes an idea only. It has not been tested on a real system. Patent pending. Suggested keywords: multi-agent AI; LLM orchestration; early warning; critical slowing down; AI safety; coordinator model; drift
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly blurs the boundary between real and synthetic visual media, determining whether online content is authentic has become more difficult. This study examines how Reddit users collectively make sense of suspected AI-generated visual content, including images and videos. Rather than assessing detection accuracy, we examine how users judge whether visual content is real or AI-generated. Analyzing 89,697 Reddit comments from AI-focused communities, we identify four major forms of authenticity reasoning: real-world plausibility, visual artifact inspection, source-based assessment, and intuition. Real-world plausibility and visual artifact inspection were the most frequently used strategies, while source-based assessment appeared less often. Authenticity judgments also did not necessarily converge over time. Instead, discussions often diverged as users introduced competing interpretations. These findings suggest that evaluating visual AI-generated content is not simply an individual detection task, but a platformed sensemaking process shaped by users’ reasoning, intuition, and interactions with others.

For most of the history of schooling, producing a piece of work was taken as proof that a learner could do the thinking behind it. Generative AI has broken that assumption. A competent essay, solution or report can now be produced in seconds, and agentic tools can complete whole courses inside a learning platform. Schools and universities have responded mostly by trying to detect AI use, a strategy that research shows is unreliable and biased against non-native English writers. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside research on detection, assessment validity and high- stakes examinations. It argues that the integrity problem is better understood as a validity problem: the question is not whether a student used AI, but whether an assessment still gives trustworthy evidence of what the student can do. The article sets out the evidence on student use and teacher perceptions, explains why detection fails, describes how single high-stakes examinations have become fragile in 2026, and docu‐ ments assessment designs used in practice, including process portfolios, supervised components, local and personal tasks, oral defence, iterative feedback and source constraints. It proposes an "evidence chain" frame‐ work of five questions that any task should answer, and identifies equity risks in the move to oral and process-based assessment that schools need to manage.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is frequently presented as a linguistic equalizer in workplaces where English mediates recruitment, collaboration, documentation, and customer interaction. Productivity research partly supports this claim, particularly for less-experienced workers. This conceptual piece argues that such gains do not constitute linguistic equality and that, for business communication scholarship, the key issue is how GenAI redistributes communicative authority, adaptation, and credibility within organizations. I call this process Algorithmically Mediated Unequal Englishes (AMUE). It operates through four connected mechanisms: normative compression into AI-polished English, unequal linguistic and affective labor, automated misrecognition and screening, and a credibility trap surrounding authorship and disclosure. These mechanisms offer resources while preserving institutional ‘standards’ and listener expectations. Linguistically equitable AI governance must therefore move beyond providing access to tools. It must redefine effective communication through task relevance, intelligibility, accuracy, reciprocal accommodation, worker control over voice, and institutional responsibility for technological risk.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Students’ attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly recognized as critical drivers of engagement in AI-supported learning. However, the extent to which these attitudes translate into perceived AI competence remains insufficiently understood, particularly within differentiated curricular contexts. Drawing on an integrated Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT) and Opportunity-to-Learn (OTL) perspective, this study examines the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and perceived AI competence and investigates whether this relationship varies across academic tracks. Rather than conceptualizing academic tracks as opportunity-to-learn itself, academic tracks are treated as proxy indicators of differentiated curricular affordances, AI-related exposure, and learning opportunities. AI attitude is conceptualized as a multidimensional construct reflecting exploration, determination, and collaboration, while AI competence captures students’ perceived cognitive, ethical, and applied capabilities in engaging with AI systems. Survey data collected from school students across varied academic tracks were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by Multi-Group Analysis (MGA), endogeneity assessment, and predictive evaluation using PLS-Predict. The findings show that students with more positive attitudes toward AI reported higher perceived AI competence, but this association varied across academic tracks. This suggests that attitudes alone do not translate into competence uniformly; rather, their association with perceived competence may vary according to the learning opportunities available within students’ curricular contexts. Robustness checks indicated no evidence of endogeneity bias and supported the model’s predictive relevance. In essence, the study contributes to AI education research by integrating EVT and OTL into a unified explanatory perspective and by positioning academic tracks as contextual proxies for opportunity-to-learn conditions that shape how students’ value-based engagement develops into AI competence.

Organizations influence almost every aspect of contemporary life. As employees, managers, customers, citizens, patients, students and members of communities, we constantly interact with organizations that shape opportunities, decisions and outcomes. Understanding organizations, therefore, requires more than examining internal structures and processes; it also requires understanding the broader social, economic, political, technological and cultural contexts in which they operate. This introductory chapter explains why understanding organizations is essential in a world marked by growing complexity, digitalization, artificial intelligence, sustainability challenges and global interdependence. It introduces organization studies as a multidisciplinary field drawing on perspectives from management, sociology, psychology, political science and economics. Key themes include organizations as social systems, value creation, organizational purpose, context, stakeholders and the relationship between organizations and society. By highlighting how organizations both shape and are shaped by their environments, the chapter lays the foundation for the book’s broader exploration of organizational structures, culture, leadership, power, collaboration, change and strategy. It encourages readers to develop analytical insight and critical reflection on organizations in an increasingly interconnected world.

Generative artificial intelligence poses well-documented challenges for university assessment. Less examined is what happens when expertise about these challenges is brought to bear in practice. Drawing on workshops in which assessment researchers worked with educators redesigning assessments after AI, we show that the advisory encounter broke down in ways we had not previously experienced. Problems refused to stabilise under advice, proposed responses triggered legitimate competing concerns, and no suggestion could obviously produce the closure that educators sought. We argue this reflects a responsibility asymmetry amplified by AI’s particular wickedness. Researchers and other experts can inform judgement but cannot bear the consequences of decisions that educators must enact now, under real institutional and ethical constraints. We call the resulting responses ‘wicked solutions’—not failed advice, but the predictable outcome of offering expert guidance on problems that resist resolution.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies is reshaping cognitive, emotional, and psychological well-being. This chapter synthesizes interdisciplinary research from psychology, neuroscience, organizational behavior, sociology, and AI ethics to examine how AI-driven environments contribute to anxiety, burnout, technostress, digital fatigue, and emotional strain. It explores the neurobiological and behavioral effects of sustained digital engagement, including disrupted attention, sleep disturbances, and altered decision-making. The chapter highlights the importance of emotional awareness, empathy, and digital self-regulation while arguing that individual resilience alone is insufficient. Aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Goal 3, it advocates systemic reforms in AI design, governance, and institutional practices to support human well-being and sustainable digital futures.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The article examines the economic aspects of applying artificial intelligence technologies and business analytics tools to enhance the profitability of enterprises operating in the field of information and communication technologies (ICT). The study substantiates the necessity of transitioning from traditional management approaches to data-driven decision-making models based on big data analytics, machine learning, and predictive analytics. It has been established that the implementation of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Business Intelligence (BI), Big Data Analytics, and Predictive Analytics enables enterprises to improve labour productivity, reduce operating costs, enhance the quality of managerial decision-making, optimize resource utilization, and ensure sustainable growth in financial performance. These technologies contribute to increasing the adaptability of enterprises to dynamic market conditions while strengthening their competitive advantages in the digital economy. The paper analyzes current trends in the digital transformation of ICT enterprises and identifies the key economic effects resulting from the implementation of intelligent information systems. A conceptual model illustrating the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on enterprise profitability is proposed. The model is based on the optimization of business processes, risk management, demand forecasting, efficient resource allocation, and strategic decision support. The practical significance of the research lies in the possibility of applying the proposed approaches while developing digital transformation strategies aimed at improving the economic efficiency and profitability of enterprises in the information and communication technology sector.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In the current conditions of digital transformation of society, innovative governance acquires the status of one of the key factors in the modernization of the public administration system. The dynamic development of information and communication technologies, the spread of digital platforms, e-government tools, artificial intelligence, big data and other digital solutions significantly change the mechanisms of interaction between state authorities, local governments, business and civil society. Under these conditions, traditional models of public administration are gradually transforming into more open, adaptive, customer-oriented and innovative governance systems capable of ensuring high quality public services, effective management decision-making and sustainable socio-economic development. In addition, innovative governance is considered as a comprehensive concept that combines modern management approaches, digital technologies, institutional innovations, partnership between authorities, the public and business, as well as mechanisms for joint development and implementation of management decisions. Its implementation contributes to increasing the transparency of government activities, developing open data, ensuring accountability, strengthening citizens' trust in state institutions, and forming an effective public administration system. The paper substantiates that innovative governance is a qualitatively new stage in the development of public administration, characterized by the use of digital technologies to optimize administrative procedures, automate management processes, develop electronic services, ensure transparency and openness of government activities, and expand opportunities for public participation in the formation of public policy. Particular attention is paid to the development of digital platforms for interaction between the state and citizens, the use of open data technologies, e-democracy, digital identification, interagency electronic interaction, as well as the application of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and big data analytics technologies in the processes of making management decisions. It is established that the modernization of the public administration system in the context of digitalization involves not only the introduction of modern information technologies, but also a comprehensive reform of the institutional environment, updating regulatory and legal support, the development of digital competencies of civil servants, the formation of an innovative organizational culture, and increasing the level of cybersecurity. At the same time, digital transformation creates new challenges related to personal data protection, digital inequality, information security, the need to ensure the ethical use of artificial intelligence technologies, and guaranteeing the digital rights of citizens. It has been proven that the effective implementation of innovative governance ensures increased efficiency of public authorities, reduction of administrative costs, optimization of administrative service provision processes, increased efficiency of management decisions, expansion of opportunities for public participation and strengthening of democratic governance. Of particular importance is the integration of the principles of openness, transparency, accountability, partnership, innovation and people-centeredness into the functioning of the modern public administration system.

The article examines the transformation of the thematic landscape of artificial intelligence (AI) in management and identifies its structural changes. The empirical basis of the study comprises metadata from scientific articles indexed in the Scopus database and selected using the PRISMA methodology. The methodological framework combines bibliometric analysis, keyword co-occurrence analysis, network visualization, thematic clustering, and a comparison of the absolute and relative representation of research clusters across the periods 2019–2022 and 2023–2025. The findings reveal an acceleration in research on AI in management, accompanied by a broader thematic scope and an expansion of international research collaboration. Network analysis identified four interconnected thematic clusters covering technological and analytical support for managerial decision-making; human resource, knowledge, and organizational process management; operations, project, and risk management; and responsible AI governance, ethics, and regulation. Strong interconnections between these clusters indicate the gradual emergence of an integrated approach to studying AI in management. The comparison between the two periods reveals a structural reconfiguration of research priorities: while all thematic areas demonstrate absolute growth, the relative dominance of technology-oriented research has declined, whereas attention to organizational, human, ethical, and regulatory dimensions has increased. Particularly dynamic growth is observed in research related to generative AI, human–AI interaction, innovation, digital transformation, sustainability, and responsible management. The findings demonstrate an evolutionary shift in research focus from the technological and operational application of AI toward its managerial and organizational integration, followed by the emergence of responsible and human-centered approaches. The results provide a foundation for further research on managerial capabilities for AI integration, models of interaction between humans and intelligent systems, and mechanisms for the responsible use of AI.

documents.abstract: Título: Uso de Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación (TIC) y su Asociación con las Dimensiones del Pensamiento Crítico en Discentes de Educación Superior: Un Estudio Mixto Explicativo Antecedentes: En la era digital, la omnipresencia de las Tecnologías de la Información y la Comunicación (TIC) y la irrupción de la Inteligencia Artificial Generativa (IAGen) han transformado los entornos de aprendizaje en salud. En el Internado Rotatorio de Pregrado, el personal médico en adiestramiento enfrenta una constante sobrecarga informativa (infoxicación) e interacción con herramientas automatizadas. Un uso puramente instrumental o delegativo de las TIC puede comprometer el desarrollo de competencias cognitivas de orden superior, mientras que un uso epistémico puede potenciar el análisis, la inferencia, la evaluación y la autorregulación clínica. Objetivo: Determinar la asociación entre los patrones de uso de las TIC (incluyendo la IAGen y la alfabetización informacional) y el nivel de desarrollo de las dimensiones del pensamiento crítico en Médicos Internos de Pregrado (MIP) en unidades de segundo nivel de atención del IMSS, e interpretar los procesos metacognitivos subyacentes desde la perspectiva estudiantil. Material y Métodos: Estudio mixto con Diseño Secuencial Explicativo (DEXPLI). · Fase 1 (Cuantitativa): Diseño multicéntrico, observacional, transversal y analítico en tres sedes (HGZ No. 53, HGZ No. 197 y HGZ No. 71, OOAD Estado de México Oriente). Se incluirá por censo a la plantilla total de MIP. Se aplicará la Escala Multidimensional de Patrones de Uso de TIC (\alpha = 0.87) y un cuestionario estandarizado de dimensiones de Pensamiento Crítico (Facione). Se realizarán análisis descriptivos, correlación de Pearson, ANOVA multicéntrico y modelos de Regresión Lineal Múltiple. · Fase 2 (Cualitativa): Abordaje fenomenológico interpretativo mediante 4 grupos focales (n = 32 MIP) estructurados por muestreo intencional de casos extremos según los cuartiles de desempeño de la Fase 1 (Q_1 y Q_4). Los testimonios serán transcritos y analizados categorialmente mediante codificación temática en ATLAS.ti para triangular las meta-inferencias. Resultados Esperados: Se prevé identificar una asociación positiva y estadísticamente significativa entre el uso epistémico de TIC/IAGen y puntajes elevados en las dimensiones de análisis, inferencia y autorregulación. Asimismo, se espera caracterizar cómo la delegación cognitiva pasiva se vincula con un menor rendimiento crítico y cómo la alfabetización informacional mitiga la infoxicación en la toma de decisiones clínicas. Conclusiones: La investigación aportará evidencia empírica clave para la optimización tecno-pedagógica de los planes de estudio del Internado Rotatorio, permitiendo establecer lineamientos éticos y metodológicos para la integración reflexiva de las TIC e IAGen en el IMSS. Palabras Clave (DeCS): Tecnología de la Información; Pensamiento; Educación Médica; Inteligencia Artificial; Internado y Residencia; Toma de Decisiones Clínicas. Structured Abstract (English) Title: Use of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) and Its Association with Critical Thinking Dimensions in Higher Education Students: An Explanatory Mixed-Methods Study Background: In the digital era, the ubiquity of Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) and the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) have reshaped medical learning environments. During Undergraduate Rotating Internship, medical interns face continuous information overload (infoxication) and interaction with automated tools. A purely instrumental or delegative use of ICT may hinder high-order cognitive development, whereas epistemic use can foster clinical analysis, inference, evaluation, and self-regulation. Objective: To determine the association between ICT usage patterns (including GenAI and information literacy) and the development level of critical thinking dimensions in Undergraduate Medical Interns (MIP) across second-level IMSS hospitals, and to interpret underlying metacognitive processes from the students' perspective. Material and Methods: A mixed-methods study with an Explanatory Sequential Design (DEXPLI). · Phase 1 (Quantitative): Multicenter, observational, cross-sectional, analytical study across three sites (General Zone Hospital No. 53, No. 197, and No. 71, OOAD Estado de México Oriente). Total population sampling of active interns will be conducted. Instruments: Multidimensional ICT Usage Patterns Scale (\alpha = 0.87) and a standardized Critical Thinking Dimensions Scale (Facione). Statistical analysis: descriptive metrics, Pearson correlation, multicenter ANOVA, and Multiple Linear Regression models. · Phase 2 (Qualitative): Interpretive phenomenological approach using 4 focus groups (n = 32 interns) selected via purposive extreme-case sampling based on Phase 1 performance quartiles (Q_1 and Q_4). Focus group transcripts will undergo thematic analysis and matrix coding using ATLAS.ti to build integrated meta-inferences. Expected Results: We expect to demonstrate a statistically significant positive association between epistemic ICT/GenAI usage and higher scores in analysis, inference, and self-regulation. Additionally, qualitative analysis will elucidate how passive cognitive delegation links to lower critical performance and how information literacy buffers infoxication during clinical decision-making. Conclusions: This study will provide key empirical evidence to optimize techno-pedagogical curricula for medical internships, informing institutional policies and ethical guidelines for the reflective integration of ICT and GenAI within IMSS training programs. Keywords (MeSH): Information Technology; Thinking; Education, Medical; Artificial Intelligence; Internship and Residency; Clinical Decision-Making.

360° MDL (the Multidimensional Literature Review Model) is a methodology for conducting and reporting literature reviews that create value, not just volume. It tells researchers where to look (five evidence stream families: academic databases, influential scholars, industry practice, policy and global organisations, and emerging and diverse voices), what to keep (the 6R Quality Gate and CCD Curation for Complementarity, Coverage and Diversity), how to analyse (eight standard analysis matrices, M1–M8), how sure to be (Triangulation Strength, Resilience Index and a Leave-One-Stream-Out test) and what value to create (Interpretation & Exploitation and an evidence-traced Value-Based Framework). The methodology comes in three tiers: Lite for doctoral students and thesis chapters, Standard for journal review articles, and Advanced for flagship and policy reviews. All three share the 3 × 3 Rule: at least three source streams × at least three analysis matrices. It includes a 30-item reporting checklist (MDL-RC 2026) and a flow diagram compatible with PRISMA 2020, so it complements PRISMA rather than replacing it. This release contains:• Methodology Overview: the full description of the method• Researcher Handbook: step-by-step guidelines, rubrics, checklists and a protocol template• Quick Start Guide and one-page Quick Reference Card: a ready-to-use route in 10 steps for researchers and doctoral students• Excel Toolkit (blank and a worked example) with live calculation of all indices• 24 figures (PNG and vector PDF) and an illustrative example review on smart cities About the author: Professor Miltiadis D. Lytras is Full Professor of Information Systems and Digital Transformation at Deree, The American University of Greece, and Research Professor at Effat University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. He holds a BSc in Informatics, an MBA and a PhD in Knowledge Management and e-Learning from the Athens University of Economics and Business. His research spans knowledge management, data science, artificial intelligence, the semantic web, technology-enhanced learning and digital transformation. He has served as Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal on Semantic Web and Information Systems, has guest-edited more than 85 special issues in Web of Science-indexed journals, and has authored or edited more than 80 international books. He has been listed among the world's top computer scientists by Guide2Research and among leading scientists in the AD Scientific Index, and he has served as Distinguished Scientist at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah. 360° MDL distils more than two decades of his experience in editing, reviewing and writing literature reviews into an open, citable methodology. How to cite: Lytras, M. D. (2026). 360° MDL: The Multidimensional Literature Review Model — Version 2026. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23724393 Researchers who use the methodology are invited to state in their methods section: "This review was conducted and reported according to the 360° MDL methodology, Version 2026 (Lytras, 2026)."

This paper presents a phase-based, real-time four-dimensional (4D) reconstruction of ancient Troy, enhanced by artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted interpretive interaction with selected virtual characters. Defined by nine superimposed settlement layers, Troy presents particular challenges for conventional two-dimensional (2D) documentation and static three-dimensional (3D) representations, especially when communicating long-term urban transformation to specialist and non-specialist audiences. To address this challenge, all nine principal phases were reconstructed as spatially aligned but separately managed layers within a single Unreal Engine 5 environment. Excavation records, stratigraphic documentation, published archaeological interpretations, and architectural reference drawings were converted into evidence-based 3D models in Autodesk 3ds Max and optimized for real-time visualization. The interpretive component uses retrieval-grounded generative conversational AI, implemented through Convai, for selected phase-aware non-player characters (NPCs). Each character is linked to curated, phase-specific historical knowledge and constrained by a defined speaking scope, contextual prompts, and response rules. The AI was not used to generate archaeological geometry, determine architectural form, or create unrestricted historical narratives. Instead, it supports contextual explanation, visitor orientation, educational mediation, and phase-specific readability while remaining subordinate to the archaeological evidence. The workflow also separates documented, inferred, and speculative elements so that uncertainty can be communicated without presenting every visual decision as equally certain. The project demonstrates that a phase-based real-time environment, combined with carefully bounded conversational AI and virtual reality (VR) interaction, can improve comparative understanding of a multi-layer archaeological site while maintaining archaeological traceability, technical performance, and interpretative transparency. Furthermore, the proposed workflow establishes a reproducible framework for integrating archaeological documentation, immersive visualization, and AI-assisted interpretation within a single interactive environment. By allowing users to examine each settlement phase independently while preserving their spatial correspondence, the system facilitates clearer observation of architectural continuity and transformation over time while supporting transparent scholarly communication, heritage education, future comparative research, and informed public engagement.

Sentiment analysis is a task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that detects polarity, opinions, emotions, or attitudes in text data. Traditional systems based on lexicons and hand-crafted features are relatively straightforward, but their adaptability is constrained by vocabulary, context, domain differences, and linguistic variation. Deep learning introduced CNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, and attention-based representations, while transformer-based pre-trained language models significantly improved contextual transfer. Transfer learning reduces the cost of target-domain annotation by leveraging knowledge from a source domain or a pre-trained model for a target sentiment task. This review examines transfer-learning methods for sentiment analysis, focusing on machine learning, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, Hugging Face Transformers, BERT, and the fine-tuning of pre-trained language models. The literature is organized into transfer-learning taxonomy, model development, BERT-based modifications, hybrid architectures, datasets, evaluation approaches, limitations, and emerging parameter-efficient techniques. The analysis highlights research gaps in source-domain selection, negative-transfer detection, low-resource and code-mixed evaluation, computational efficiency, explainability, continual adaptation, and reproducibility. The review suggests that promising future systems should not focus solely on increasing model size, but should identify relevant knowledge, adapt effectively, and maintain robustness across diverse domains and languages.

Artificial intelligence is becoming part of routine business judgment. Firms use it to identify customers, screen job applicants, anticipate demand, evaluate credit and prepare managerial reports. These applications promise speed and scale. They also create difficult questions about fairness, privacy, worker dignity, accountability and the public consequences of automated decisions. This conceptual paper examines how responsible artificial intelligence can be translated into ethical business practices rather than treated as a separate compliance exercise. Drawing on recent peer-reviewed research published primarily between 2024 and 2026, the discussion connects stakeholder responsibility, organizational governance and the practical management of AI systems. It identifies six business-facing ethical obligations and develops a proposed framework linking leadership commitment, risk-sensitive design, human oversight, stakeholder voice and continuing assurance to ethical outcomes. The paper argues that a responsible firm does more than publish AI principles. It determines where AI should be used, records who remains answerable for each decision and creates a workable route for challenge and correction. The framework is presented as a set of conceptual propositions for subsequent empirical testing. Implications are discussed for managers, auditors, policymakers and smaller firms with limited technical capacity. The central conclusion is that responsible AI is best understood as an ongoing organizational capability that protects human interests while enabling legitimate business innovation

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves into a foundational infrastructure of future civilization, concerns surrounding AI governance extend beyond technological capability and existential risk. This declaration argues that the defining challenge of the AI era lies in the potential concentration of intelligence infrastructure and the resulting concentration of cognitive influence within a limited number of technological ecosystems. While vertically integrated AI systems may accelerate innovation, they may also create new forms of structural dependence that threaten individual and societal freedom. To address these emerging risks, the paper introduces three interrelated concepts: Technological Sovereignty, defined as freedom from dependence on a single technological ecosystem; Cognitive Sovereignty, understood as the ability to maintain meaningful control over one's own processes of thought and judgment; and Ontological Autonomy, the capacity to remain the author of one's own existence in an increasingly AI-mediated world. Building upon the framework of On-Site Adaptive Innovation (OAI), the declaration emphasizes the importance of decentralized adaptive capabilities and the democratization of intelligence infrastructure. It concludes that the future of AI will be shaped not only by the power of intelligent systems but also by the governance structures that determine access to and control of intelligence itself. Preserving technological plurality, cognitive freedom, and human autonomy is therefore presented as a fundamental prerequisite for maintaining freedom in the age of artificial intelligence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
